text.text: Adura had learned to read the room before she learned to read words. She watched the shoulders of her father when the letters from the bank arrived, and she knew before the envelope was opened that the answer would be no. By twelve she could tell which of her parents' silences meant anger and which meant simply tiredness, and she had already decided that growing up meant becoming the person who asked the questions nobody else thought to ask. It was not curiosity that drove her, exactly. It was the suspicion that adults were accustomed to a version of events that did not survive being examined too closely.

The principal was not an unkind man, but he believed that the business of a school was discipline before it was instruction, and that a boy who had been properly taught to hold his tongue would learn more in a year than one who had been permitted to argue with his teacher. In this he was consistent to the point of severity, and the whole school understood that the first law of the assembly hall was silence, and the second was attention.

The boy was born before his parents actually got married and so the court had declared him .... Within a year the family had left the village, and by the time he was old enough to ask questions of his own he had learned that there were things about his own beginnings that adults preferred to discuss in a lowered voice.

The harmattan arrives in Kano the way an uninvited guest arrives at a naming ceremony — loudly, without apology, and impossible to ignore. By mid-December the dust has settled into every crevice of the city: the sills of windows that have not been opened in weeks, the folds of wrappers hung out to dry, the keyboards of the cybercafés along Zoo Road. Traders wrap their wares in polythene and complain, as they complain every year, that business has slowed to a crawl. Yet there is a stubborn festivity to it as well. Children chase one another through the haze, shrieking at the sting of it in their eyes, while their grandmothers sit in doorways wrapped to the eyebrows and pronounce, with the authority of long experience, that this year's dust is worse than last year's.

Public libraries in Nigeria were once the quiet engines of ambition. A student with no money for textbooks could .... a whole education between their shelves, and many did. Today those same buildings stand .... in most cities, their collections outdated and their roofs leaking. The tragedy is not only the decay of the buildings but the .... of the habit they sustained — the daily, unhurried encounter with books that no examination syllabus can replace.
